fatal_errors: The proposed larger 45–75 μm feedstock is not the demonstrated intervention; the target used finer 5–30 μm powder with an optimized low-temperature ID-HVAF i7 process.

Keeping spray parameters unchanged while increasing particle size can produce incompletely molten particles, poor flattening, greater porosity, and reduced deposition efficiency rather than a thicker intact coating.
The cited evidence does not demonstrate that increasing feedstock size increases coating thickness or deposition efficiency while preserving low oxidation.
The experiment does not test oxidation performance under the relevant 1000–1150 °C, 50 h isothermal service conditions.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the stated thickness shortfall and gives a clear two-group falsification experiment, but it does not reconstruct the successful intervention or operating window. The demonstrated solution was an approximately 150 μm coating made from fine powder using optimized medium-pressure, low-temperature ID-HVAF spraying, yielding 79% deposition efficiency, 0.2% porosity, phase retention, and minimal as-sprayed oxidation. The proposed particle-size mechanism is only partly plausible: lower specific surface area can reduce in-flight oxidation, but larger particles require sufficient heating and may remain partially molten when all other parameters are fixed. E1 supports only the general role of specific surface area in oxidation, while E2 reports acceptable splat formation for an appropriate powder and provides no comparative evidence favoring larger particles. The design measures deposition quality adequately but omits the key high-temperature alumina-TGO, internal-oxidation, mass-gain, and spallation tests needed to establish bond-coat service integrity.
